Methods: a specialist pain clinic added fortnightly pharmacist telephone calls to physician-led tapering and compared patients who started a taper in the 12 months before the change (n = 94) with those who started in the 12 months after it (n = 101). Results: in the after period, 58 percent of patients reached a 25 percent reduction in daily dose at six months, against 37 percent before. Mean pain interference scores did not change in either period. Eleven percent of patients left care within six months after the change, against 24 percent before. Conclusions: pharmacist telephone support was followed by more dose reduction and fewer patients leaving care; a concurrent comparison is needed."},{"title":"Voluntary opioid tapering and pain interference over 12 months: a prospective observational study in two pain clinics","authors":"Castellane-Obi D, Frey-Mwangi L","year":2023,"venue":"Tessary Journal of Pain Care","doi":"10.5555/tjpc.2023.0088","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We followed 212 adults who chose to taper long-term opioid therapy in two specialist pain clinics, with outcomes collected at routine visits every three months. Over 12 months, the mean daily dose fell by 41 percent. Pain interference with daily activities, rated from 0 to 10, improved from a mean of 6.8 at baseline to 6.1 at 12 months, and 19 percent of patients paused or reversed their taper at least once. Patients with moderate or severe depression at baseline had smaller improvements in pain interference. Twelve-month data were missing for 14 percent of patients, mostly those who had stopped attending. The absence of a comparison group limits causal interpretation."},{"title":"Overdose and withdrawal-related emergency visits after opioid dose reduction: a population study of dispensing data","authors":"Nakagawa-Brent S, Adeyemi-Holt K, Rasmussen-Lowe T","year":2019,"venue":"Northreach Epidemiology Reports","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Using regional dispensing and hospital data for 33,400 adults on stable long-term opioid therapy, we compared periods after a dose reduction with periods of stable dosing. In the two months after a reduction of more than 20 percent per month, overdose or withdrawal-related emergency visits were 1.7 times as frequent as during stable dosing. After slower reductions of 10 percent per month or less there was no measurable excess. The excess was concentrated among patients who received no follow-up contact within four weeks of the reduction. Confounding by the reasons for dose reduction cannot be excluded, and dispensing data do not show what patients actually took."},{"title":"Patient-centred interventions for opioid tapering: a systematic review of dose, pain and safety outcomes","authors":"Whitcombe-Diallo A, Sorensen-Okafor B, Ibarra-Lund C, Petrov-Achebe M","year":2020,"venue":"Clinical Tapering Review","doi":"10.5555/ctr.2020.0311","providerType":"review","abstract":"We searched four bibliographic databases to 2019 for studies of interventions supporting voluntary opioid tapering in adults with chronic non-cancer pain. Twenty-seven studies met the inclusion criteria, only five with a concurrent comparison group. Multidisciplinary support with frequent contact was associated with greater dose reduction, and pain and function were stable or improved in most studies. Only six studies reported overdose or emergency visits. Definitions of a successful taper ranged from a 25 percent reduction to complete discontinuation, which prevented pooling. Most studies were at high risk of bias from selection and loss to follow-up."},{"title":"Who leaves an opioid tapering programme? Distance, language and disengagement in a regional pain service","authors":"Okonjo-Lindqvist R, Barros-Hale E","year":2024,"venue":"Journal of Rural Pain Services","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We reviewed clinic data for 176 adults who started a supported opioid taper in a regional pain service between 2019 and 2022. Disengagement, defined as no contact for six weeks, occurred within six months in 31 percent of patients living more than 60 km from the clinic and in 15 percent of those living closer. Patients who needed an interpreter disengaged about twice as often as other patients. Among distant patients, those offered telephone contact every two weeks disengaged less often than those offered clinic visits only. Distance and language were recorded routinely, but reasons for leaving were rarely documented."},{"title":"A brief telephone checklist for withdrawal symptoms during slow outpatient opioid tapers: agreement with clinic assessment","authors":"Delacroix-Nguyen H, Mbatha-Ross F","year":2022,"venue":"Tessary Journal of Pain Care","doi":"10.5555/tjpc.2022.0147","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Withdrawal symptoms during slow tapers are usually assessed only at clinic visits. We developed an eight-item checklist that a pharmacist can administer by telephone in about three minutes and compared it with a clinician's in-clinic assessment on the same day in 84 patients. Agreement was good (intraclass correlation 0.81), and repeated telephone checks showed that symptoms peaked two to five days after each dose step. Patients preferred the telephone check to extra clinic visits. The checklist has not been tested in patients with limited English or in rapid tapers."},{"title":"Collaborative pharmacist and physician tapering in primary care: a controlled study across 18 practices","authors":"Hollis-Mensah G, Varga-Tanaka I, Oduya-Pereira L","year":2016,"venue":"Primary Care Pharmacy Quarterly","doi":"10.5555/pcpq.2016.0056","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Eighteen primary care practices were allocated by region to collaborative tapering, in which a practice pharmacist and physician agreed a taper plan and reviewed it monthly, or to usual care. At 12 months, 28 percent of patients in intervention practices had reduced their daily dose by at least 30 percent, against 17 percent in usual-care practices. Emergency visits did not differ between groups. Allocation was not random, intervention practices were larger, and patients were recruited from primary care rather than specialist pain clinics, so the findings may not transfer to patients referred for complex pain."}]}
